div.head: Cn 1027 Inscr.
div.ab: Cnuto rex totius Anglię et Denemarcię et Norreganorum et partis Suanorum Æthelnotho metropolitano et Alfrico Eboracensi archiepiscopo omnibusque episcopis et primatibus et toti genti Anglorum tam nobilibus quam plebeiis salutem.

Canutus, rex totius Angliae et Denemarciae et Norreganorum et partis Suanorum, Æthelnotho metropolitano et Alfrico Eboracensi archiepiscopo omnibusque episcopis et primatibus et toti genti Anglorum tam nobilibus quam plebeiis, salutem.

Canute, King of all England and Denmark and of Norway and part of Sweden, to Æthelnoth the Metropolitan, and to Ælfric, Archbishop of York, and to all the bishops and notables and the whole of the English nation, both nobles and commoners, greeting.

Cnut, king of all England, and of Denmark, and of the Norwegians, and of part of the Swedes, sends greeting to Æthelnoth the metropolitan, and to Ælfric, archbishop of York, and to all the bishops and leading men, and to the whole race of the English, whether nobles or ceorls.
div.note: Latin only (Cnut's letter of 1027, c. May; Latin translation c. 1070–1100, the Old English original is lost). Liebermann's text is from Florence of Worcester (ed. note.seg: It is this letter, preserved only in Latin translation in the chronicles of Florence of Worcester and William of Malmesbury, that allows us to date Cnut’s journey to Rome, for the coronation of the Emperor Conrad by Pope John XIX on Easter day (26 March), 1027, is certainly the assembly referred to in paragraph 5 of the letter. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle dates Cnut's journey to Rome 1031, and this has led Campbell (Encomium Emmae Reginae, pp. lxii f.) to argue that Cnut made two journeys to Rome. But see p. 255, n. 5. The letter is of outstanding importance for our knowledge of Cnut's reign, of his international dealings, his troubles in Scandinavia, and his concern from abroad for the governance of England, and it also shows that foreign trade was considerable enough for the king to interest himself in it. It is to be regretted that the Old English version has not survived. We do not know where Florence and William got their information that the bearer of the letter was Lifing, then abbot of Tavistock (see No. 9, p. 314), but there may have been a.rubric to the text of the letter. If, however, we accept the statement that Lifing was not yet a bishop, we must reject the date of a charter in the Codex Wintoniensis (Kemble, No. 743) in which he appears as bishop already in 1026. The letter is edited by Liebermann, I, 276–7, and with English translation by Robertson, pp. 146–53. It is given in Thorpe’s edition of Florence, I, 185–9, and in Stubbs’s edition of William of Malmesbury, I, 221–4. For translations of these works, see pp. 303, 310. [Her footnote 7: No. 49 in the 1955 edition]

ealles Englalandes stand wohl im Orig., wie I Cn Pro und Urk. a. 1023 Ke 737, im Ggs. zu Cnuts Teilherrschaft neben Eadmund II. 1016, vielleicht aber auch zum Königstitel (s. d. Gl 4 ff.) 10. Jhs., der die Bestandteile des Reiches genannt hatte. Urkk. mit totius Anglie, oder Britannie oder Albionis oder gentis Angligenae sind Ke 728. 730. 734 ff. 741. 743 f. 746. 750 f. 753. 1316. Denemarciae ist vielleicht des Stils wegen nur durch den Übersetzer angeglichen; im Orig. stand dafür Dena, das Volk, nicht das Land. Cnut erwähnt Dani c. 6, vielleicht Angloskandinaven, weil in dem Einen regnum, meinend, dagegen c. 10 mehrere regna und wiederholt verschiedene populi unter seiner Gewalt

ealles Englalandes probably stood in the original, as in I Cn Pro and the charter of the year 1023 Ke 737, in contrast to Cnut's partial rule alongside Edmund II in 1016, but perhaps also to the royal title (see the Glossary s.v. 4 ff.) of the 10th century, which had named the component parts of the realm. Charters with totius Anglie, or Britannie or Albionis or gentis Angligenae are Ke 728. 730. 734 ff. 741. 743 f. 746. 750 f. 753. 1316. Denemarciae has perhaps been assimilated only by the translator, for the sake of style; the original had instead Dena, the people, not the land. Cnut mentions Dani in c. 6, perhaps meaning Anglo-Scandinavians, because [he is] in the one regnum; on the other hand in c. 10 [he mentions] several regna and repeatedly various populi under his rule

‘Norwegen und Teil Schwedens’ erkennt als spätere Zufügung schon Lappenberg Gesch. v. Engl. I 476; Pauli Mon. Germ., SS XIII 126. (Eine ähnliche vollzog ein Schreiber um 1100 zu I Cn Pro) Dies wiederholte ein Crowlander Fälscher; s. o. Einl. 1. Erst 1028 eroberte Cnut Norwegen; s. d. Gl 4. — Statt Suanorum wollen bessern Sclavorum Suhm, Steenstrup (Normannerne III 327. 329), Hunt, Larson (Canute 152. 344), wogegen sich Bresslau (Konrad II. II 142) mit Recht erklärt. Auf Münzen (Parsons Brit. numism. soci. Apr. 1914) nennt sich Cnut rex Sueuorum, so dass Worsaae (Danske Erobr. 325) den Titel für echt hält. Vom rex Danorum et Norweynensium spricht Giso von Wells um 1030 Hist. episc. Somerset. Die Vie s. Edward behauptet, vielleicht aus Cn 1027: En ses escritz au cumencement se fist numer Cnut rei des Engleis, de Norweie, de Daneis, de Escoce [?] et de Suane sire; ed. Luard p. 30. Das Encomium Emmae (Mon. Germ. 19, 520) zählt fünf Reiche Cnuts, mit Britannia, Scotia, ohne Sclavia oder Schweden, mancher Nordische Autor 6, darunter Sclaviam (Mon. Germ. 29, 33. 65. 68. 165. 170, wo die Ostseeländer bis Samland und Esthland spezialisiert sind) oder die Inseln (Corpus poet. boreale II 155. 157). Vgl. über Cnuts Slavische Eroberungen Bresslau I 101. 246

‘Norway and part of Sweden’ was already recognized as a later addition by Lappenberg Gesch. v. Engl. I 476; Pauli Mon. Germ., SS XIII 126. (A similar one was made by a scribe c. 1100 to I Cn Pro.) A Crowland forger repeated this; see above, Introduction 1. Cnut conquered Norway only in 1028; see the Glossary s.v. 4. — Instead of Suanorum, Suhm, Steenstrup (Normannerne III 327. 329), Hunt, Larson (Canute 152. 344) wish to emend to Sclavorum, against which Bresslau (Konrad II. II 142) rightly declares himself. On coins (Parsons Brit. numism. soci. Apr. 1914) Cnut calls himself rex Sueuorum, so that Worsaae (Danske Erobr. 325) considers the title genuine. Giso of Wells c. 1030 Hist. episc. Somerset. speaks of the rex Danorum et Norweynensium. The Vie s. Edward asserts, perhaps from Cn 1027: En ses escritz au cumencement se fist numer Cnut rei des Engleis, de Norweie, de Daneis, de Escoce [?] et de Suane sire; ed. Luard p. 30. The Encomium Emmae (Mon. Germ. 19, 520) counts five kingdoms of Cnut, with Britannia, Scotia, without Sclavia or Sweden; many a Norse author counts 6, among them Sclaviam (Mon. Germ. 29, 33. 65. 68. 165. 170, where the Baltic lands as far as Samland and Estonia are specified) or the Islands (Corpus poet. boreale II 155. 157). Cf. on Cnut's Slavic conquests Bresslau I 101. 246
